title: Sony Music moves to add more than 30,000 copyrighted recordings to its lawsuit against Udio

reading.body:
The core failure here is one of training-data provenance: an AI music generation system was built using copyrighted recordings without the rights holders' authorization. This happened at the model-building stage, before any product reached users, meaning the legal and ethical problem was embedded in the system from the start. No licensing check or rights-clearance process was in place before the training corpus was assembled.

The dispute involves multiple major record labels, a class action from independent artists, and a musicians' union lawsuit, showing that the affected parties span the full range of music rights holders. Universal Music Group and Warner Music Group each settled and entered licensing arrangements with Udio, while Sony Music filed a separate new lawsuit alleging unauthorized use of more than 30,000 recordings. A court declined to dismiss the independent artists' class action and transferred it to a different jurisdiction rather than ending it.

None of the lawsuits have produced a final verdict on liability, and the settlements do not constitute admissions of wrongdoing. What is established is that the training-data question is the central dispute across all proceedings, and that the only mechanism now agreed upon to resolve the problem going forward is licensing, not a technical fix to the model itself.

summary:
Universal Music Group has settled a lawsuit against AI music startup Udio by reaching licensing agreements. UMG had accused Udio of using copyrighted songs to train its artificial intelligence system that generates original music from text prompts. The settlement requires Udio to launch a new platform next year trained only on authorized and licensed music, allowing users to customize, stream and share songs. Financial terms were not disclosed.

UMG, Sony Music, Warner Music Group and others had sued Udio, claiming it improperly used hit songs like The Temptations' "My Girl" to create similar compositions without permission or payment. Udio countered that its AI learns from musical examples the way students study scores. This represents Udio's first licensing deal with a major record label. UMG's CEO stated the agreement demonstrates the company's commitment to supporting artists and developing new business models, while Udio's founder called it an opportunity to unite AI and the music industry.
